intended_object: The standard Weyl group representative n_α = w_α(1) = x_α(1) x_{-α}(−1) x_α(1) attached to a root α (Steinberg, Carter §6.4). Here it is taken as an A-point, for any commutative ring A, of the Chevalley-type group (the "Kostant toral closure") built from the root subgroups x_i(t) = exp(t·ρ(e_i)) acting on an admissible lattice. This comes from the docstring and the module documentation.
explanation:
The body is the product of three root-subgroup points in the toral-closure subgroup: x_i(1)·x_j(−1)·x_i(1). Here `kostantToralRootSubgroupPoints i A` is the divided-power exponential homomorphism t ↦ exp(t·ρ(e_i)) from the additive group of A (written as `Multiplicative A`), restricted to land in the carrier subgroup. This is exactly the classical formula w_α(t) = x_α(t) x_{−α}(−t⁻¹) x_α(t) at t = 1, which is Carter's and Steinberg's n_α.

The docstring says plainly that i and j are meant to be opposite roots of an sl₂ pair. That hypothesis (hT) is only needed for the conjugation theorems in the same file, and those theorems check the expected behaviour:
- n x_i(u) n⁻¹ = x_j(−u);
- n normalizes the torus;
- n acts on the torus by the reflection attached to the root.

Leaving the hypothesis out of the definition is a harmless generalization, not a mistake.

The generality is the one in which the surrounding Chevalley-group construction is set up. The construction works over an arbitrary commutative ring A, which is the natural generality for points of a group scheme. Mathlib has no Chevalley groups and no Weyl representatives of this kind, so it has no more general counterpart.
